utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We'll get to the questions, which I will try to answer briefly, and of course I'm here for any further questions. The first one on my note was responding to the Gvero argument that Article 49 of the Geneva Conventions is the ruling article on this point and that it applies only to civilians. Well, we agree that Article 49 of the 1949 Geneva Conventions applies to civilians only, but that is, of course, not where the discussion and the analysis stops. We can also see that Common Article 3 of those conventions refers to "hors de combat" and does not limit it to civilians. But most importantly, we look, as has the Appellate Chamber looked, to customary international law, and as we look at Mrksic and Martic, that the Appellate Chamber has a long discussion on customary international law, citing the various authorities over the years that have stood for and expanded the original view beyond just civilians. I would draw your attention in Martic, particularly, to paragraphs 305, 306, 309, and 311, where they lay out some of that customary international law. And just for an example, that we have not been held solely in this Tribunal to Article 49, Article 49 has required that for deportations, they be deported from occupied territory. Well, that has never been a requirement in this Tribunal. Not that it has to do with this case, but that's just an example of how this Tribunal, through its Article 5, has expanded the scope from the Geneva Conventions from 1949. Okay. The next question I see is that in the Miletic brief there was an allegation that we did not specifically refer in the indictment to Miletic's role in restricting the UNPROFOR resupply convoys, and where we did specifically refer to his role in restricting the humanitarian convoys. Well, I don't believe that is correct because if you go to the indictment, under paragraph 75, where we specifically describe some of General Miletic's actions, we note that Miletic, acting individually or in concert with other members of the joint criminal enterprise to forcibly transfer and deport the populations of Srebrenica and Zepa, and knowing that forcing the Muslims out of the enclaves was unlawful, committed acts in furtherance of the joint criminal enterprise as ascribed in paragraphs 50 to 54 of this indictment and below." And then under the heading "Making Life Unbearable for the Inhabitants of the Enclave." We go on to say under I: "He drafted Directive 7 which was signed by President Karadzic on 8th March and called on the VRS to inter alia ..." And then we lay out the two foundational points of this case, the forcible transfer and how it began: One, the policy to create an unbearable situation so life was impossible for the Muslims and, two, the issuing of permits to reduce and limit the logistical support for UNPROFOR and the supply and material resources to the Muslims. So there it is. Now, yes, it is first noted that he drafted that, but we're not just putting that down as merely the drafter. Of course, we are holding him and the others in the joint criminal enterprise for carrying that out, and there it is spelled in black and white, reducing UNPROFOR. Now, the next "(ii)" we particularly point out and emphasise the part about the Muslim restriction, but that should not be viewed to suggest he's not responsible for all of Directive 7 and particularly the part where it says "reducing the help to UNPROFOR." And, in fact, as I'm sure you're aware, the whole thrust of our case is -- regarding UNPROFOR is not so much that UNPROFOR is a victim in this case, but it's their reducing the fuel and other supplies and the reinforcements to UNPROFOR that directly affects UNPROFOR's ability to look after and protect and do their duty regarding the Muslim population. So as we focus on the Muslim population, that's, of course, the focus, but we also clearly point out UNPROFOR and the reason that UNPROFOR is so important is not for UNPROFOR on its own, but UNPROFOR as it relates to the Muslims. Now, it's not just the indictment that lays this out. We may not remember much of my opening statement back in the 21st of August, 2006, but what I attempted to do in a very short opening statement, as you may recall, is point out the specific and important links of the accused to this case, and I went accused by accused by accused. And I want to read to you -- when I got to the Miletic section, and I read out one of the convoy documents where General Miletic had made some specific restrictions on the inspection of cargo and fuel tanks, and then I said this: "Now --" and for the record, this is on page 443 back on the 21st of August, 2006: "Now, this shows that General Miletic is playing a very important role in this. Now, on its face, there is nothing criminal about this, but it does indicate to us the role he's playing, and he can say to the Zvornik Brigade, 'I demand a detailed ...' Now, is that an order from a commander? No. Is it a directive you have to follow? Yes. This is consistent with Mladic's overall order Directive 7 and the other materials that we've seen establishing the policy. And you'll see, speaking of fuel, how fuel was restricted and strangled. So by the time DutchBat was there in July, when these events happened, they didn't have enough fuel to run their air-conditioning or their electrical, and they couldn't go out in the vehicles, and this is all the Main Staff's doing through their corps, through their brigades, as it was done with General Miletic." Now, that's pretty clear. General Miletic is involved in the restriction against UNPROFOR, both in the indictment, right up front in the opening statement. An indictment can't possibly list all the ways in which people commit crimes. We did our best, you required us to do even better, and this indictment does a good job of it. And also in Miletic's brief, they make the conclusion that -- regarding the location of Miletic and Milovanovic in 1995. Now, the exhibit that I would draw your attention to, and as cited by the Defence, but not very accurately, is P03163, and this is a little information report done right before Milovanovic -- I believe right before he testified, where we went over with him this complete collection that we had of reports from the Main Staff to the president, and those reports were -- came out in the name of Miletic or Milovanovic and sometimes others signing "Za" for them, and he went through all of those and noticed his name and Miletic's name and other's name, and he went through -- and from that document you can see the conclusions of that, and he testified that basically this represents the time that he would have been there or Miletic would have been standing in for him. It's not perfect. You may recall there was -- Ms. Fauveau showed Mr. Butler, I think it was on the same day, one document that went out in Milovanovic's name, one that went out in Miletic's name. As Milovanovic goes to a front and comes back, that this is clearly not going to be absolutely 100 per cent representative, but it does give you a good idea of the long periods of time that Miletic was standing in, and some of the periods of time that Milovanovic came back. So just very roughly we can see from this document that for most of January, it was signed off by Miletic. I counted, this morning, nine days in February that was Miletic. The rest of it was Milovanovic. Six days in March that was Miletic. Mostly the rest of March, it was Milovanovic. Seven days in April was Miletic. May, it was a rough split. And then from 31 May all the way to 4 September, it's all Miletic. And also recall, when Miletic comes back, he's not always in the HQ. Sometimes he's within Zvornik, looking after -- excuse me, when Milovanovic comes back, he's not always in the headquarters. Sometimes he was in Zvornik, looking after an operation in that area. And when he does come back, he's going to be briefed and they're going to have to communicate very closely with each other. So -- and this is engaging General Miletic in the briefing as well. So when Milovanovic doesn't come -- when he comes back, that doesn't disengage Miletic. In fact, if General Miletic was the chief of the air force defence, perhaps he would have been slightly more disengaged, but he, as chief of operations, he is not going anywhere. He's fully engaged in all this material. So there's no real lack of knowledge or action on Miletic's part when Milovanovic comes back. Yes, he would not be standing in for -- in this informal way that we have described and you're the experts on now, when Milovanovic is back, but that doesn't fundamentally change the equation here. In fact, it shows they're both working together. All right. There was another question regarding the adjudicated -- your adjudicated facts decision and whether that shifted the burden of proof, and I gave you my recollections on that, that -- at the time that I didn't -- none of us felt that there was any obstacle put forward by the Trial Chamber for either side on these adjudicated facts; that they were an attempt, of course, to stream-line the case. And we found the language which reflects just that, and it's from 27 September 2006, page 2253. And, Mr. President, you said, starting at line 3: "Basically, the decision means, first, that in as far as those 250-odd adjudicated facts that we have agreed with you upon, the Trial Chamber is simply taking judicial notice of the fact that that fact was adjudicated by a previous Trial Chamber. We are not going any further than that. The fact that a previous Trial Chamber has adjudicated that on the 11th of July, 1995, the VRS entered into Srebrenica does not mean that the chapter begins there and finishes there, and that you are -- neither of you, nor the Defence, are entitled to expand on that. There are some adjudicated facts that obviously go in favour of your case, and there are several adjudicated facts that go in favour of the Defence. What we have stated there is what I have told you, and if you need to expand on that to make things clear, because ultimately it's we who will have to adjudicate not only on that fact, but all the facts that are pertinent, of course you will be able." I think that it more than clearly establishes you're not putting the adjudicated facts in the way of anybody. They are free to put on their case, and that, of course, is consistent with the entire way you've run this case. We don't see authoritarian moves to block anyone in three years, which I'm sure is very much appreciated. And the last note that I have had to do with Mr. Borovcanin's claim that we have not charged him with aiding and abetting; specifically, had not charged him for aiding and abetting in the failure to protect the section. This can be answered very simply by going to the section on individual criminal responsibility. It's paragraph 88 of the indictment, where we say: "Pursuant to Article 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal ...," and we list everyone, including Borovcanin, "... are individually responsible for the crimes charged against them in this indictment, and each of them committed, planned, instigated, ordered, and otherwise aided and abetted in the planning, preparation, and execution of these charged crimes as set out in detail in this indictment." But then we go on and repeat ourselves in more particularity, and we speak especially regarding Mr. Borovcanin in paragraph 92, and we say: "As a separate and independent basis of liability under 7(1), Ljubomir Borovcanin's presence at or near the Kravica warehouse execution site, described in paragraphs 30.4 and 43(A)(iii) of this indictment, together with his failure to intercede in order to protect prisoners there, instigated, assisted, and aided and abetted the physical perpetrators of the killings in that his presence served as encouragement and incitement to the physical perpetrators of the Kravica executions who continued to kill prisoners during and after Ljubomir Borovcanin's presence." We go on to the second part of that: "... and, (b), constituted a willful failure to discharge his legal duty, resulting in liability under 7(1) as an omission, in that Ljubomir Borovcanin had custody and control over 1.000 Muslim prisoners held in the Kravica warehouse on the afternoon and evening of 13 July. He had a legal duty to protect those prisoners from harm from his own troops and others, including at least one member of the Bratunac Brigade Red Berets. Despite his ability to do so, Ljubomir Borovcanin failed to protect all the prisoners within his control who were held at the Kravica warehouse." Now, the beginning of that paragraph mentions aiding and abetting regarding both those two, his presence as an encouragement and incitement and his failure in his duty to protect. And I would just add one brief comment about this idea of aiding and abetting. "Aiding and abetting" has been defined as knowing of the criminal event and substantially assisting in it, intending to provide substantial assistance in it. Now, when determining the intent of an individual that hasn't confessed or made admissions, this is precisely how a prosecutor or anyone, a trier of fact, determines intent; that the accused knows about a crime and that he was part of it. Where Trial Chambers draw the line between aiding and abetting and actual intent, it's very difficult to determine. It's up to the individual Trial Chamber. There's no clear jurisprudence on that. The sentencing between the two, aiding and the abetting and actual intention, has not been very different, if you look and see what Krstic was sentenced to as an intentional participant and what Krstic was sentenced to as an aider and abetter. I think one was 45, 46 years and the other was 35. So they're not viewed as particularly different, because, well, obviously they're not. When you intentionally take part and provide a substantial assistance to a crime, you're a key member of it. And none of these are individual crimes. They're all working together. This idea that there's one central figure and all the rest are elves, and you have to determine who's most responsible, well, that's a matter, in our view, of sentencing. And so when you look at the evidence of knowledge of the crime and substantial assistance to it, you should infer, in my view, that one intends the known consequences of one's acts. You can, in fact, find that one intends the natural and probable consequences of one's acts. When human beings act and they know that the likely consequences of their acts are a crime, a horrible crime such as murder, you may infer that they intend to do that. That's the way we humans are. I don't think we need to get, in this case, into the likely consequences, because when Mr. Borovcanin does not act, he knows that's going to result in deaths, whether by bleeding to death at the warehouse or further executions or both. So please consider those words as you consider this very difficult but yet crucial area for international law. We are this far in the Tribunal, and we still have not clearly defined what it is that there's a difference, though the case law clearly says the desire is not a requirement. We don't have to prove that they want this to happen. Many times, people commit crimes and they don't want or desire to have done that, but they do it because they have to do it. It happens. So that was the last. I think it was clear that there was no -- in the indictment, there was nothing in the indictment suggesting that Mr. Beara participated in the reburials, so he cannot be held responsible under the indictment for that. There may have been a witness that mentioned his name regarding the reburials, and I think that evidence is in the case, but there's nothing wrong with that. But we absolutely stand by what we had said and what Your Honour had said before. So I think I've gotten most of them or -- if not all of them, and stand prepared to answer anymore questions, or sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Mr. McCloskey. We can now start with the closing arguments of the Popovic Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. You've got two hours and a half, as you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Popovic Defence filed its final brief and elaborated, within the limits set out by the Trial Chamber, its position on the indictment, crime-based testimony, so the witnesses' expert findings and exhibits. I skip to this paragraph. The time allocated for the closing statement does not give me the opportunity to elaborate on all the arguments set out by the Prosecution in its final brief. As a result, I'm going to restrict my closing statement to the part of the Prosecution final brief addressing the responsibility of Vujadin Popovic. The Prosecution's assertion in paragraph 2320 of the final brief, that Popovic was reassigned to the Drina Corps as the chief of the Intelligence and Security Department in November 1992, is incorrect. It relies on the testimony of the witness Mikajlo Mitrovic. This testimony was clearly misconstrued by the Prosecution, as it did not mean that Popovic became the head of the Intelligence and Security Department of the Drina Corps Command once he was reassigned there. Popovic initially became an ordinary officer in this department and then was reassigned to the 2nd Romanija Brigade, where he spent approximately one year and a half. Thereafter, he was sent on a course for security officers in Pancevo, and only after that was he assigned to the position of the chief of the Security Department of the Drina Corps Command in early 1995. The witness Vojnovic supports this when he testified that he worked with Popovic for a year or a year and a half when he was the security officer of the 2nd Romanija Brigade. It is transcript page 23712, 21st July 2008. The document by the Drina Corps Command of 11 May 1994 - it is 7D485 - was signed by Lieutenant-Colonel Ranko Kuljanin in the capacity of the Drina Corps chief of the Intelligence and Security Department, further supports it. The enumerated evidence clearly indicates that Popovic was not chief of the Intelligence and Security Department before 1995. Also, the reorganisation or, precisely, separation of the intelligence from the security organ took place in 1995, not 1993, as the Prosecution final brief states. This is evident in the fact that the previously-mentioned Drina Corps document reads that in 1994, the Intelligence and Security Departments were in the same organ. In the next paragraphs, the Prosecution analyses various rules and documents to prove the responsibility of Popovic, but for prisoners of war and refugees, as well as his duty to coordinate with MUP. The Prosecution's arguments and analyses of these subjects are incorrect. The submission on Popovic responsibility for prisoners of war is based on two grounds. First of these grounds are the legal norms assigning to the military police the physical security of prisoners of war. The Prosecution submits that Popovic participated in the organisation and implementation of the measures for the security support. The security support includes, among other things, the military police measures. One of the military police measures was the direct security of prisoners of war and the guidance and control of the movement of refugees. It's paragraph 2328 of the Prosecution's final brief. Since Popovic allegedly had a duty to control the military police units, but from the corps command and the subordinate brigades, he was responsible for both prisoners of war and refugees. Secondly, the Prosecution asserts that the corps security chief was responsible for prisoners of war because he proposed to his commander ways in which the military police would be used, was authorised to direct the commander of the military police units in accomplishing the tasks ordered by the unit command, and had control of the military police units at the corps and brigade levels. The Prosecution's assertions were founded on distorted facts and misinterpretation of relevant rules and documents. The first rule misconstrued by the Prosecution is the rule of corps. It's 7DP412. According to paragraph 468 of the rule of corps, security support includes five kinds of measures, one of which were counter-intelligence measures and activities. These measures are within the exclusive competence of the security organs and at the level of the Drina Corps Command, of which Popovic was solely responsible for. These are the measures provided by paragraph 6 of the Rules of Service of the security organs. It's P407, assigning the counter-intelligence works to the security organs as protagonists. All other security measures, including military police measures, were in the exclusive competence of the unit commander. These are command and staff tasks stipulated by paragraph 7 of the Rules of Service of the security organs. In these tasks, the security organ participate -- that is, the need for his participation or extent of such participation is determined exclusively by the commander on a case-by-case basis. In this sense, the participation of Popovic in security support, as the security organ, is different from counter-intelligence measures; as such, cannot be taken for granted or assumed, but must be proven on a case-by-case basis. This means that the Prosecution must prove not only that Popovic was authorised to participate in military police measures relating to security support, but that he really participated in the military police measures relating to security support -- sorry, but that he really participated in the organisation and implementation of such measures because such participation was not obligatory, according to the rules. It means that the Prosecution must prove that Popovic participated in military police measures relating exactly to the prisoners of war and/or refugees in the relevant period. For example, Popovic could have participated in the organisation and implementation of just one of the military police measures, say, in direct security of the Main Staff commander, General Mladic, in the Operation Action Uda [phoen]. It is P0033. However, this doesn't mean that he participated in all other military police measures and, in particular, those related to prisoners of war and refugees. The Prosecution did not prove that Popovic was ordered by his commander to participate in military police measures related to prisoners of war or refugees in the period relevant for the indictment. The Prosecution also used an incomplete quotation and misleading interpretation of Article 29 of the Regulation regarding responsibility of corps command. It is 7DP410. The Prosecution quoted in paragraph 2324 of its final brief only the part of sentence that the security organ of the corps is responsible, I quote: "... for organising and implementing security measures and undertaking other specialised work in the field of security ..." However, the sentence continues as follows: "... that is placed under its responsibility by special regulation, et cetera." The omitted part of the sentence limits the responsibility of Popovic to security measures placed under his responsibility by special regulations. The special regulations were incorporated in the rule of service of the security organs. These special regulations made him responsible for counter-intelligence work, not for organising and implementing the measures of the whole security support, including military police measures and, in particular, those regarding prisoners of war and refugees. Accordingly, he was only responsible for professional management and control of the military police, not for the control of all its activities and duties. Professional management of the military police --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suggest you keep some water handy, nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Professional management of the military police was precisely defined by paragraph 14 of the Rules of Service of the military police and include the organisation for education and training, inspection of such training, taking part in drafting and establishment of military police units, preparation of the relevant rules and regulation, and taking part in the control and assessment of the combat readiness of the military police units. The responsibility for the other four kinds of security support is provided by Article 9 of the same regulation. According to section 6 of this provision, the corps commander is in charge of managing security service, responsible for the security support of the command and subordinate units, and institution and taking measures on the basis of the regulation and his responsibilities. The Prosecution submission that corps security organ had the duty to control the whole work of the military police units of the corps command and subordinate units is contrary to the principles of the military organisation for VRS established in this case. The main principle in the organisation of command is the principle of the singleness of command. I refer to Vuga, transcript 4 July 2008, pages 316 to 334. It was the supreme principle, meaning that the commander of a military unit has an indivisible and exclusive right to command all subordinate units and bears responsibility for the condition, combat readiness, and use of the units, as well as for the proper execution of all tasks assigned to the unit. I refer to Kosovac. It is 16 January 2009, page 224. In fact, the command function places three main duties and obligations on the commander: to take a decision; to issue an order; and to control or monitor or follow up on what he has ordered. I refer to Forca. It's 20 June 2008, page 586, lines 3 to 10. The Prosecution's interpretation of Article 29 and submission that Popovic was responsible for the security support and the control of the military police would mean that the brigade commanders issued orders to their military police units, but could not control whether they carried out such orders properly or not, because the corps security chief was authorised to control military police. In all aspects of their work, including the execution of orders issued by the brigade commanders, such an approach would be in contravention with the principle of the singleness of the command by practically excluding the military police units from the effective command of the brigade commander. Anyway, item 9 restricts the professional management of the security organ as regard the control of the work of the military police just within the limits placed under the responsibility of the security organs by special regulation as provided by the first paragraph of Article 29. The absence of the duty of the Drina Corps security chief to control the whole work of the military police units of the corps command and subordinate units is endorsed by the fact that there was no regular daily reporting of these units to the security organ of the Drina Corps. For general and daily control of the activities of the military police, it was necessary for the subordinate units to submit regular reports. However, there is no evidence to support that the military police units from the brigades were under a duty to send such report -- regular reports to the security organ of the Drina Corps; neither is there evidence to support that they did so at all. They submitted daily reports to the commanders of their brigades, as did all other units. The brigade commanders did not also have any obligation to inform either their own security officer or the security organ from the corps command about orders given to the military police unit of his brigade or about the daily activities of these units. Without such reports, the security organ of the Drina Corps was not able to know anything about the activities of the military police on a daily basis. This proves that the security organ of the Drina Corps had no duty to control all the work of military police units, but at corps or brigade levels. Otherwise, the line of regular reporting would have been established between the military police units of the brigades and corps and the chief of the security organ of the Drina Corps Command. The special regulations contained in Rule of Service of the security organs provides two kinds of their duties. The first group is counter-intelligence work, and the second administrative and staff work. The counter-intelligence work had to be performed by the security organ without any order from his commander. The practical impact of such a provision on this case is that the Prosecution had no need to prove that such work in the Drina Corps Command was performed by Popovic, since he was the only individual carrying out the work, was not authorised to transfer such duties to anyone else, and the commander of the Drina Corps was not authorised to give this kind of work to any other officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise to interpreters. The second group of duties which includes military police tasks was to be carried out only upon the order or request of the unit commander. I refer to Vuga. It's transcript page -- 30 June, 2008; transcript page 057 to 058. For this group of tasks, the commander of the unit was exclusively authorised to decide whether the security organ would be included in the decision-making process relating to ways of using the military police units. I refer to paragraph 2324 of the Prosecution final brief. This further means that the commander of the unit was not duty-bound to seek a proposal from his security organ on ways of using military police units, but only when he deemed it necessary. He was not bound to inform the security organ of what tasks and orders he issued to the commander of the military police units. Again, Vuga; it is pages 058 to 062. In this sense, it was not obligatory that the commander of the unit assigns the task to its military police unit through the security organ, as stated in Prosecution paragraph 2325. It is also incorrect to assert that the security organ always directed the commander of the military police unit in accomplishing the tasks issued by the commander of the unit. He did so only if the unit commander found it necessary. Otherwise, the unit commander assigned the task to the military police commander, without any participation on the part of the security organ. In addition, the chief of security of the corps is responsible to the corps commander for the activity of the military police unit in the corps command pursuant to paragraph 23 of rules only when such activity stands from the tasks issued upon his proposal. Otherwise, he cannot assume responsibility for the tasks issued by the corps commander to the military police commander without his knowledge. This is quite logical, as the security organ could propose the use of the military police only within the scope of his activities which relates to counter-intelligence work. All other use of military police via the physical security of persons and features could be proposed by the commander of the military police who is the best trained and qualified for such tasks. I refer to expert report of Vuga, paragraph 2.90. Of course, the commander of the unit is authorised to assign any task and issue order to the military police unit without asking or even contrary to the proposals made either by the security organ or military police commander. In short, it cannot be taken as the rule that the security organ effectively participated in the organisation and implementation of measures, other than that of counter-intelligence. According to the Rule of Service of security organs, paragraph 7(e), the security organs participate also in, I quote: "... in operations that precede the initiation of criminal proceedings, and criminal proceedings themselves," et cetera. It is, again, the expert report of Vuga. It is 1175 -- 1D1175, paragraph 244. These duties are among the command and staff duties for which command organs are responsible and in which the security organ participate. It means that commander determines the scope of such activity, who will do that, military police or security organ, or both of them, when and whether the report will be sent directly to the Prosecution or to the high-ranking officer, and whether such information will be sent at all. In this light, the military prosecution guide-lines the Prosecution indicates in its final brief does not replace the legal obligations and relationship in the command of the VRS provided by Rule of Service of the security organs and the Law on Military Courts. Namely, the Prosecution quote the obligation of Popovic to receive reports about crimes and report of any information up the chain of command. There is no evidence that Popovic received any report or that he failed to report the information about crimes up the chain of the command. Because of that, Popovic could not be responsible as the Prosecution states in paragraph 2409. In addition, the Prosecution refers to some documents indicating that the chief of security of the corps had a duty for the control of the military police units, but in the corps and subordinate brigades. The work plan of the Drina Corps for the 10th of December, 1994 - it is 5D989 - tasked the chief of security with the control of the work of the military police units from the corps command and the subordinate units. However, the authors of the plan knew what kind of control over military police the security organs were authorised to perform. This document was intended for officers who knew very well the scope of their competence. As such, it was not necessary to write down in this particular document the various rules and regulations determining the nature, scope, and limits of the security organ's control over the military police. This plan did not exclude either corps commander or brigade commander from the control of their military police units, meaning that the control of security organ was restricted to the professional management. The Prosecution also misinterpreted three documents sent by security organ of the Drina Corps Command as evidence of Popovic competence concerning prisoners of war and his authority over the military police. The first was the instruction regarding the handling of prisoners of war, dated 15 April, 1995. It is P196. In fact, this was the instruction of the Security Administration of the Main Staff concerning the security aspects of the handling of prisoners of war. It was observed that after exchange, prisoners of war became significant sources of highly-sensitive military information about VRS for the enemy's intelligence. This was because before direct exchange, they were kept near the front-line or military objects with full insight into the deployment of VRS forces and units, their arms and other data. The instructions alerted the commands from the battalion level upwards to determine places behind the front-line where kept members of the enemy's army were to be kept and warned that such, I quote: "A place must not be in the area of a command post, nor in the area of communication centres, artillery weapons, or significant elements of logistic support." Accordingly, this instruction does not demonstrate the responsibility of security organ for prisoners of war, but the counter-intelligence measures which had to be applied by the commands to the third intelligence activities of enemy forces and counter-intelligence protection of material, technical equipment, zones, areas, and features of particular importance. These were the duties for which the security organs were protagonist as provided in paragraph 6(a) and (c) of the Rules of Service of security organs. It's P407. The parts quoted by the Prosecution are, in fact, measures preventing prisoners of war from observing VRS units deployed in the vicinity, their arms, and other features relevant for the defence of Republika Srpska. In addition, the text of this instruction clearly indicates that Popovic literally conveyed the instruction of the Main Staff Security Administration and, therefore, could not indicate his responsibility for prisoners of war, basically. This was a clear example of the professional management defined by paragraph 14 of the Rules of Service of the military police. This paragraph includes, among other things, the education, training, and preparation of the military police members, preparation of the rules and regulations related to the military police. This instruction is an elaborated regulation on how to handle prisoners of war and keep them as far as possible from sensitive military information. Popovic was bound to forward any instruction received from the superior security organ to the subordinate units, and this document just demonstrates that he did so. In addition, this document clearly demonstrates the competence of the unit commands for prisoners of war. This is indicated in paragraph 2, which reads, I quote: "All commands from battalion level upwards are to determine places behind the front-line at which captured members of the enemy army are to be kept." They further advise what kind of risk should be avoided from a counter-intelligence point of view. The second document the Prosecution refers to is dated 7 February 1995. It's P3032. This document was sent by the security organ of the Drina Corps Command to brigade commands. This was again based on a request made by the Main Staff Security Administration, seeking information about the management of the military police in subordinate units, their level of training, mobilisation, logistics -- logistic support, security, and tasks. The document properly reflects the limits of the competence of the security organs over the military police. It also reflects the fact that the chief of security of the Drina Corps Command sought information necessary for professional management of brigades' military police units from the brigade commands, not directly from the military police units of the brigades. If Popovic had overall control over the work of the military police units of the corps command or subordinate units, he would have asked for such information directly and not through the brigade commands. The Prosecution also misrepresented document 3D436, which was the instruction sent to the chiefs of security and intelligence of the 5th Military Police Battalion of the Command of the Drina Corps subordinate brigades regarding the work of the military police check-points. The Prosecution found, notably, that Popovic assigned to the chiefs of security and military police commands in subordinate units responsibility for the implementation of the instructions. This is contained in reference 5074 of the last evidence. However, the document literally conveys the instruction of the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS, General Mladic, who pointed out - it is paragraph E, on the last page just above the signature of General Mladic - that, I quote: "Assistants for security intelligence duties of the VRS Main Staff, corps commanders, and their subordinate organs and units of military police are responsibile to me," meaning General Mladic, "for due implementation and acting upon this instruction." The sentence added by Popovic was that chiefs of security in the units and commanders of the military police units are responsible to this department for the implementation of this instruction. This could only mean that the assignment of responsibility which the Prosecution wrote about derives from the specific order of the corps commander to make responsible for the implementation of this instruction the security organs and military police commanders of the subordinate unit --

However, it doesn't mean that the corps commander made either the security organs or military police commanders from the subordinate units responsible for all their work through security organ of the corps. It actually indicates that this was the case only whenever he decided so, and this was stressed in document sent to subordinate units. The Prosecution also misinterpreted the order dated 30 August 1995 concerning the disarming of UNPROFOR. It is 7DP978. This order was issued upon the order of the Main Staff of the Security Administration and was not sent to the military police unit or security organs of the subordinate brigades, but to the commands of the brigades. This meant that Popovic intended to stress to the brigade commands the importance of the task because he was not able to issue any order to the brigade commanders. In fact, it was the request to the commanders that they issue requested order to their subordinates. The Prosecution further misrepresented the role of Popovic in the assignment of the tasks to the military police. He did not assign all tasks to the military police unit approved by his commander, but only those assigned upon his proposal within his purview or if he was asked by his commander to give some professional advice based on the counter-intelligence information and -- available only to him. Even then, his commander could issue the order to the commander of the military police unit directly without his involvement. For all other tasks, the commander of the unit issued the order directly to military police commanders and not to Popovic. I would -- I'll go to another topic, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I move on, the role of security in Krivaja 1995 and this operation. The Prosecution submission of the decision by the command to murder all Muslim men and boys contravenes the evidence in this case. The task of the Krivaja 95 operation was to separate the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves. It is P107. In military terms, it was one-axis operation in a very narrow area, without any ambition to encircle the enemy's troops and take prisoners. Such action usually result in taking of sporadic individual prisoners. The numeric strength of VRS forces assigned for the operation was not adequate for the encirclement and capture of enemy forces; namely, the VRS deployed about 2.000 soldiers for the action, while 28 Division had more than 10.000 soldiers. I refer to Lasic. It's 4th June 2008, pages 734 to 736. The encircling and capturing of the enemy forces required at least three times as many. This means that strength of troops assigned to the operation and the nature of the very operation was not intended at killings, but on the separation of enclaves. The evidence also demonstrates that after the task was extended to include the take-over of Srebrenica, additional troops were not sent which would have allowed for the encirclement, capture, and killing of members of the 28th Division. This means that such a decision was not made either before or after the fall of Srebrenica. The VRS entered Srebrenica after it had been completely deserted by its population and despite having knowledge of the fact that the 28th Division had mobilised all its forces and was trying to break through to B and H territory, made no considerable effort to engage all its troops for the purpose of blocking, encircling, and capturing of ABiH forces. On the contrary, the VRS immediately sent a major of its troops who had been participating in the Srebrenica operation to Zepa, which was on the opposite direction of the movement by the 28th Division, leaving Zvornik almost undefended. The aforementioned facts clearly show that there was no evidence that VRS command made any decision to murder all Bosnian men and boys from Srebrenica, as stated in paragraph 261 -- 67, sorry, of the Prosecution final brief and paragraph 24 of the indictment. The test given to security organs in this operation was adapted to the goal of the separation of the enclave. The Krivaja 95 operation task was completed on 9 July 1995, when the enclaves were separated. There is no evidence that any prisoners of war were taken during the action. Even after the goal of the operation was extended to the taking of Srebrenica, it did not result in the capture of prisoners. Therefore, the VRS had no enemy prisoners of war until 12th July 1995. Because of that, the submission of the Prosecution that on 11 July 1995 between two NATO bombings, Popovic spoke with General Krstic about prisoners of war is baseless. The more logical conclusion is that the only topic of their conversation, if any, could be how to survive NATO attacks. The task assigned in the Krivaja 95 order ceased once Srebrenica was taken and troops got new tasks relating to Zepa operation. The new tasks were also issued as to prisoners of war, because on 11 of July 1995, the president of Republika Srpska appointed Miroslav Deronjic as the civilian commissioner for Srebrenica. It's P10. His tasks were, among other things, to, I quote: "... ensure that all civilian and military organs treat all citizens who participated in combat against the Army of Republika Srpska as prisoners of war and ensure that the civilian population can freely choose where they will live or move to." It's paragraph 4. He was also authorised to appoint his assistants. It's paragraph 6. This was the decision of the president of Republika Srpska, who was also the supreme commander of the Armed Forces of Republika Srpska. This decision regarding the prisoners derogated and substituted the Krivaja 95 order as to responsibility of the security organs for prisoners of war and entrusted Deronjic with the authority to implement this decision. The decision came into force on 11 July 1995, on the same day when VRS entered Srebrenica. I refer to Vuga, 2nd July, page 216 to 219. The assertion of the OTP that Popovic stayed at Hotel Fontana on 13 and 14 July is not correct. The document obtained by the Defence, and later by the Prosecution, too, proves that Popovic was at the Hotel Fontana on 11 and July 12, 1995, when the Bratunac Brigade approved his stay there. It was shown during the examination of Bjelanovic. It is 11 June 2008, page 111 to 112, and on 14 November 2008 the Defence provided the Trial Chamber and the parties with the copies of all the Hotel Fontana documents, as requested by the Trial Chamber. The invoice referred to by the Prosecution did not indicate the dates he stayed at the Hotel Fontana, but instead the date when Hotel Fontana prepared the invoice and sent it to the Bratunac Brigade for payment. With reference to paragraph 2362, Popovic was in the proximity of General Mladic because he had a duty to protect him as requested pursuant to the Operation Action Uda. The action required, among other things, counter-intelligence protection of General Mladic and three other VRS generals which was in the exclusive competence of security organs. In the scope of these tasks, Popovic was in the proximity of General Mladic in Srebrenica on 11 July, at the third Hotel Fontana meeting and in Potocari on 12 July, and in Vlasenica on 13 July, when General Mladic got there on the ceremony of the hand-over of duties between General Zivanovic and General Krstic. However, at the third Hotel Fontana meeting, Popovic did not represent anyone, as stated in paragraph 2365. He attended because, as the chief of security of the Drina Corps, he got the task to provide counter-intelligence protection of the Main Staff commander in Operation Action Juda. With reference to paragraph 2363, the information that on the afternoon and the evening of 11 July, an estimated 1200 to 1500 able-bodied Muslim men arrived in Potocari was not clear. The Prosecution even asserts that there was one -- between 1.000 and 2.000 Muslim men in Potocari on 11 July and that VRS was aware of it. According to the Prosecution, they posed potential threat to the Bosnian Serb forces that were planning to enter Potocari on 12 July. It is paragraph 492 of Prosecution brief. The presence of 1.000 to 2.000 Muslim men in Potocari would not present a potential but a real and serious threat for the VRS. This is because the reconnaissance patrol could not provide information as to whether these people were armed or members of ABiH, but eventually only that they were in civilian clothing. The total strength of VRS troops engaged in the Srebrenica operation was 2.000 men. The alleged information would indicate that Muslim forces in Potocari were equal to the VRS troops engaged in the whole of Srebrenica operation. This information would, therefore, cause a serious source of concern for the VRS, since they were still well aware of the main force of the 28th Division. In such a situation, the VRS would encircle Potocari in the early morning hours on 12 July and call for the surrender of such forces. General Mladic and other high officers would not enter Potocari with camera crews and journalists knowing that 2.000 Muslim soldiers could attack them at any moment. Potocari was one of the places where a considerable number of Muslims dwelled until fall of Srebrenica. The able-bodied men being mobilised left the village to the meeting point of 28 Division in Jaglici and Susnjari before the VRS entered Potocari on 12 July. This means that they were still in Potocari on 11 July in afternoon and evening. In addition, the headquarter of 280 Brigade was also in Potocari. I refer to 4D135. This brigade defended the Srebrenica-Potocari axis and had the task to defend the industrial area in Potocari. It is P107, paragraph 1, subparagraph (3). On 6 July 1995, this unit, referred as MM Potocari, had 1.007 members. I refer to 1D607. After the fall of Srebrenica on 11 July in the afternoon, an order of 28th Division Command to withdraw its forces to Jaglici and Susnjari, the troops deployed to defend Potocari left the area on the same afternoon and evening. This meant that the number of 28 Division members passed through Potocari on their way to Jaglici and Susnjari. I refer to Rutten. It's paragraph -- it's page 837 to 838, 13 November 2006. So the VRS reconnaissance patrols could see these men in Potocari on 11 July in the afternoon and evening, and included them in the assessment. However, after the ABiH troops left Potocari to Jaglici and Susnjari, only between 400 and 700 men were noted. I refer to Momir Nikolic transcript, 22nd of April, page 009, lines 7 to 20. Due to the above, the information of 1200 to 1500 Muslim men in Potocari on 11 July 1995 was an estimate made before the members of 208 Brigade left Potocari to Jaglici and Susnjari with mobilised, able-bodied men. The number of Muslim men transported from Potocari on 12th and 13 July was exaggerated and unreliable, as specified by Witness Mile Janic. He testified in Blagojevic that on the first day only 10 to 15 buses was, with approximately 70 men in each, were dispatched from Potocari. This would mean that 700 to 1.050 men were transported on 12th July only. He further testified that on 13 July, two or three times more were dispatched. It would mean that on that day, between 1.400 and 3.150 Muslim men were transported in total. It would suggest that between 2.100 and 4.200 Bosnian Muslim men were sent from Potocari on 12th and 13 July. According to the witness, a bus had 52 to 54 seats, and 15 to 20 people were standing in aisles. It is -- his testimony is on 20 November 2007, pages 942 to 944. However, a bus full of prisoners, with just a driver in it, would present an obvious security risk for the driver. The risk would not be diminished with the presence of one or two soldiers beside the driver. They could not control the prisoners who were sitting and standing due to overcrowding. The soldier, or two of them, standing beside the driver, could not see anything but up to ten prisoners in front of him. The prisoners would be so close to him that he would not be able to prevent an attack, despite carrying arms. This, therefore, means that the VRS would not risk the lives of its personnel by overcrowding of buses with prisoners. Besides, Janic had not only task of counting Muslim men, but of counting all the refugees. He obviously was not able to carry out this task, which meant that Colonel Jankovic at one point told him that, I quote: "An average per bus was, therefore, worked out and used to calculate how many refugees were transported from Potocari." It is in Blagojevic judgement, paragraph 181, and it is in transcript in Blagojevic, 9773 and 9842. He testified also that some discrepancies in counting were observed by Colonel Jankovic, which makes both the calculation and estimates unreliable. On the other hand, the witness already told his story in Blagojevic, and the Trial Chamber did not find his estimate credible. I refer to paragraph 495 for Blagojevic judgement. His testimony just proved that he did not carry out properly the task of counting the number of persons from Potocari which he was given. The number of separated Muslim men in Potocari is not supported with OTP missing list. It is P566. The source of data is ICRC list, as indicated at page 2, last paragraph. However, it is quite unknown who provided these dates and when, as well as how much time passed before such data were provided. Namely, the date when a person was last seen is not necessarily provided by the eye-witnesses, but also got from other unknown and unreliable sources. Because of that, there is no evidence that the entries in this list in respect to date corroborate the arguments of the Prosecution that 2.000 men were separated in Potocari. The list demonstrates that 516 people were last time seen in Potocari before 12th of July. In addition, the list shows 660 Muslim men last seen in Potocari on 12 July. However, Potocari were not under VRS control before the noon on that date. The list does not demonstrate whether 660 people were last seen before or after the VRS entered Potocari. With respect to the testimony of Momir Nikolic, the Defence extensively addressed the ostensible conversation between him and Popovic in paragraphs 289 to 305 of its final brief. Now, the Defence repeats that the conversation described in parts of Nikolic testimony and the paragraph 4 of his statement of fact related to 12th July 1995 in front of the Hotel Fontana never took place. Popovic never told him that Muslim men and boys would be detained and then killed or that Muslim women and children would be transported to B and H-held testimony. This was confirmed by Kosoric, who testified that such a conversation has never taken place. Momir Nikolic did his best to court the Prosecution and said whatever he believed that the Prosecution would like to hear. He even falsely confirmed his own identity on photographs and falsely confessed that he ordered the execution in Kravica and Sandici. He agreed to tell obvious lie that the intent of the VRS in the attack on Srebrenica was to remove all Muslim population from the enclave, although upon the request of the Trial Chamber, personally wrote that such decision did not exist at the time, and confirmed it in his testimony. He even agreed to avoid any mention of the 28th Division just to give the illusion the enclave was demilitarised and the attack of VRS could not be directed at military targets. Corroborating evidence which the Prosecution mentioned was something that Momir Nikolic used to conceive his story. He was provided with all this evidence before he made his statement of fact. The picture taken in front of the Hotel Fontana does not depict Momir Nikolic with Popovic and Kosoric, but with Popovic, Colonel Jankovic and General Mladic's bodyguard. Such a picture cannot be taken as corroboration that Momir Nikolic had an alleged conversation with Popovic and Kosoric and in particular about the topic of such a conversation. The ostensible reconnaissance of Ciglane as execution site cannot corroborate the statement of Nikolic that he suggested to Popovic and Kosoric. There is no evidence for the Prosecution submission that Popovic assigned Momir Nikolic to coordinate the so-called separation of the Muslims in Potocari. Firstly, the terms "separation of Muslim men and boys from their families," or "the separation from their loved ones," were widely used in this case; their legal mis-characterisation of the arrests implemented by the VRS according to the generally-accepted norms and customs of war, such mis-characterisation is inciting the ethnical animosity and hatred towards the Serbs who carried out their duties. On the other hand, such mis-characterisation consistently conceals the fact that members of the ABiH were among the populations of Potocari, despite unchallenged evidence demonstrating that in the night between 11 and 12 July there were 300 ABiH members in the UN compound in Potocari. It is 1D463. It seems that Major Franken also permitted a certain number of men inside the compound who are or could have been active combatants. It's the testimony of Rutten, 30 November 2006, page 885, lines 15 to 21. Popovic did not assign Momir Nikolic to coordinate the separation of able-bodied Muslim men and boys and expulsion of the women and children in Potocari. The testimony of Nikolic in this regard is not only inconsistent, but in clear contravention with other evidence. According to the Witness Boering, who as professional officer of the Royal Netherlands Army, is perfectly qualified to clarify the military terms, Momir Nikolic was some sort of coordinator, as he himself indicates, for transport and separation, and that he received the authority from Colonel Jankovic. It's the page 536, transcript 25 September 2006. It is quite logical that someone who coordinates the work of different units should have the authority to do that. On the other hand, he must inform the subjects participating in the work that he was authorised to coordinate. Such persons must inform all concerned who provide him with such authorisation so that it could be checked. Momir Nikolic did it and indicated that he was authorised for coordination by Colonel Jankovic, so that anyone interested in it could check with Colonel Jankovic. It means if Momir Nikolic was authorised by Popovic to coordinate in the so-called separation and transportation of Muslims in Potocari, he would indicate Popovic as the individual who authorised him to do that and not Colonel Jankovic. Boering also testified that Jankovic's role was, first of all, to provide General Mladic with direct assistance, and that was why at one of the meetings he was seated directly next to him and occasionally he consulted with him. He also learned that Colonel Jankovic was assigned to wrap matters up on the side and behalf of General Mladic as a type of liaison from General Mladic to DutchBat, which meant he was to arrange things with DutchBat to the full execution of General Mladic's plans. He clarified that Mladic's plan meant the transport of refugees, but that it was not his personal observation, but based on insight and hearsay. It is transcript page 144 to 145, 21st September -- 21 September 2008 -- 2006, sorry. In Blagojevic, the witness testified that General Mladic introduced Colonel Jankovic as his next in command to take care of matters if General Mladic was absent. I refer to Blagojevic trial judgement, 154. Momir Nikolic testified that after the third meeting in Hotel Fontana on 12 July, he asked Colonel Jankovic what would be his next task, and he was told that he was to help during the evacuation of the people who were in Potocari. This entailed evacuation and separation of the able-bodied men who were in Potocari. It's testimony of Momir Nikolic on transcript 22nd April 2009, pages 014 to 015, and his statement of fact, paragraph 5. Momir Nikolic confirmed his testimony in Trbic case that there was no need for him to inform Colonel Jankovic about what he did in Potocari, given that Colonel Jankovic himself was deployed in Potocari and Jankovic was in charge, not him. It is transcript page 268 to 279, 27 of April, 2009. The presence of Colonel Jankovic in Potocari was confirmed by the Witness Mile Janic. He testified that early in the morning on 12 July 1995, upon the request of Momir Nikolic, he arrived at Potocari. Nikolic assigned him to Colonel Jankovic, who tasked him, before any of buses had arrived, to count the refugees who would be transported from Potocari. He got the same task the next day. This task indicates that the physical presence of Colonel Jankovic in Potocari was related to the transportation of refugees. It is transcript page 926 to 928, 20 November 2007. In the VRS, the carrying out of an order was regularly reported to superior command. The report that the evacuation had been successfully completed was submitted by Colonel Jankovic on 13 July. It's 5DP113. The report was sent from Bratunac to the Main Staff and the Drina Corps. If Popovic was tasked with coordination, this report would have been sent by him and not Colonel Jankovic. The presence of Colonel Jankovic in Potocari was also observed by DutchBat members. Franken complained to him once he got reports of -- on of abusing of the detainees in the White House. It is transcript 16 October 2006, page 499. He also asks Franken to sign the statement of evacuation. It is P453. Franken also testified that Colonel Jankovic made it clear that DutchBat members could not leave the base from 13 July until their withdrawal on 21st July. Franken also let Colonel Jankovic know about compilation of the list containing 251 Muslim men registered by the DutchBat within their compound in Potocari on 12th or 13 July, 1995. It is transcript page 502 to 503, 16 October 2006. According to van Duijn, it appeared that Colonel Jankovic was inspecting the area. It is OTP final brief paragraph 335. Finally, Momir Nikolic testified that after ostensible meeting on 12 November 1995, he did not see Popovic again on the day and that in the following days they did not communicate or do anything together. It is page 029, lines 12 to 20, 22nd April 2009. It is quite impossible to delegate a coordination assignment to someone and then have no communication with him while the work he had to coordinate was still ongoing. If the quoted evidence is true, there is no evidence to support that Popovic either coordinated the activities of various VRS or MUP units in Potocari or that he delegated this kind of work to Momir Nikolic. There is a contradiction in the testimony of Momir Nikolic when he states that he did not communicate with Drina Corps policemen at all and did not see their commander. It is page 013 to 014, 22 April 2009 - and that of the Witness Trisic, who testified that he saw the military policemen from Drina Corps providing security to the Muslims in Potocari together with Bratunac Brigade military policemen, and that Momir Nikolic coordinated their activities. It is transcript 20th of October, 2008, pages 103 to 104. It is, however -- the presence of the Drina Corps military police in Potocari was restricted to the escort of General Krstic. At that time, the military police of the Drina Corps was deployed at Kocari, not engaged in military police tasks but in the combat operation. 90 per cent of the members of the 5th Military Police Battalion of the Drina Corps Command were engaged in the combat operation in June until 7 July 1995 and further. It is 1D1078, paragraph 5. Only 13 military policemen stayed in Vlasenica to perform military police duties and carried out, in rotation, the physical security of the Drina Corps Command, escort of the commander and the chief of staff, et cetera. It is Vuga transcript, 2nd of July, 2008, page 204 to 206. However, it was quite possible that Trisic saw soldiers who had military police insignias of the Drina Corps on their uniforms. The evidence indicates that these insignias were sewed onto the uniforms so that members of the unit that were deployed to other units took with their uniforms their insignia. The Witness Bjelanovic testified that it facilitated their movement because it was much easier for them to find transportation from one place to another with such insignia. It is 10 June 2008, page 274 to 275. The problem grew to the extent that Popovic personally went to the Vezionica factory to discuss the problem with the commercial director of the factory, Slavisa Racic. They were trying to find a solution for problem with armbands instead of sewing the insignia onto the uniforms. I refer to 1D1438, 1438. It is witness statement of Slavisa Rasic. So Momir Nikolic knew the military policemen from the Drina Corps who were present in Potocari and did not communicate to them because they were escort of General Krstic and he had nothing to do with them. However, he communicated with the soldiers who were not members of the Drina Corps military police at the time but just wore these insignias, and because of that he testified that he did not communicate with military policemen of the Drina Corps. On the other hand, Trisic saw Momir Nikolic communicate with the soldiers who wore the insignias of the Drina Corps military police, but did not know that they were not at the time members of that unit. As a result of the above, the Defence admit that Momir Nikolic either communicated with escort of General Krstic or with soldiers who only wore the insignia of the Drina Corps military police but were not members of that unit. If the military police of the Drina Corps was present, except the escort of General Krstic, under his direct command, they would have their superior who would be in charge of the unit or the part of the unit deployed in Potocari. Finally, there was no way that Nikolic could issue the orders to Drina Corps military police or to the units of the Main Staff. He could not also get such an authority from Popovic. The Defence, therefore, submits that there is no evidence that Popovic had authority from his commander to coordinate the work of units in Potocari on 12th and 13 July 1995 or that he transferred such an authority to Momir Nikolic and oversaw his work there. Popovic was not involved in coordination and security of the buses. The Prosecution submits that Popovic, as the sole security officer of the Drina Corps Command at the time, was involved in logistical issues concerning the buses. There is no evidence, however, that Popovic was involved in the logistic issues concerning the buses. The buses were provided by the commander of the Drina Corps and Ministry of Defence, with the participation of the competent services of the VRS. There were -- there was no need for Popovic to leave his jobs and become involved in that of others. On the other hand, Popovic's first duty was to perform counter-intelligence work, because only the officer in the Drina Corps who was authorised to do that. The essence of Operation Action Uda was to detect the conspiracy against General Mladic and other leading officers of the VRS. In short, Popovic was competent for dealing with SIC activities against VRS and inside VRS. His participation in the security of the buses transporting Muslim population from Potocari to B and H-held territory was not ordered to do -- to do that, and it is not within his counter-intelligence work. The column of buses needed physical security only, and this was a task which the corps commander and the commanders of the units in the area had to provide. In addition, the Witness Kosoric testified that he was tasked by General Krstic to go before the first convoy of buses to Luka and convey the order of General Krstic to the unit in that area to secure the unhindered passage of refugees to Kladanj. It is page 794 to 795, 30 June 2009. This had nothing to do with security in competence of the security officer, but with physical security of opening the passage through minefields. May we move to the private session, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sure. Let's go into private session for a short while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: All these matters are in the purview of the corps commander and commanders of units deployed in the area, since such activities required physical security, and there is no evidence that any participation in this task was requested from Popovic by his commander. Finally, the deployment of patrols was within the competence of the corps commander and the commanders of subordinate units from the area along the route. As such, this submission remains unsubstantiated. Popovic was only in Potocari on 12 July afternoon for a short period, and this was when General Mladic, General Krstic, and other officers was present there. However, he had no additional task to oversee either the transport of Muslim population or the so-called separation of the Muslim men. The Prosecution submission that General Zivanovic was in Potocari is in clear contradiction with Srebrenica video, where he was not captured at all on this date. The submission of the Prosecution that Popovic saw the distribution of the bread in Potocari is also unfounded. The video the Prosecution refers to shows the distribution of bread to Muslim refugees who are inside the UN compound in Potocari by VRS soldiers and UN members. Popovic was standing between the truck, where the bread was, and the refugees, who were behind the fence. His back was toward refugees, clearly indicating that he was not overseeing the bread distribution. At one point, Popovic asked the soldiers to stop the distribution of the bread, and it seems that they complied and removed the truck to another place and resumed the same job. The video only indicates that Popovic sought that they stop of bread distribution from that point -- from that position and their removal of the truck, and not that he oversaw this distribution of the bread. If Popovic was in charge of overseeing the distribution of the bread, he would have watched the participants of the process, the soldiers who carried out the task, and refugees who got the bread. His acts just depict that at one moment the truck presented an obstacle to his task. As such, he sought its removal. Popovic did not instruct VRS soldiers in Potocari on 13 July. It is particularly unsubstantiated that Popovic was aware of intimidation, physical violence, and abuse of the Muslim population in Potocari. None of the witnesses testified that he saw Popovic at such places or that he complained to Popovic about it. It is not true that Popovic was next to the White House. The identification by Rutten was wrong, and its unreliability was obvious from the fact that he was the only one who recognised General Zivanovic as the officer who, on 12th and 13 July, was in Potocari giving instruction and in charge. On 12 July 1995, nobody but Rutten saw General Zivanovic in Potocari. We have seen him Vlasenica on the day - it's St. Petar's Day - giving the speech. He alleged that he also saw him on 13 July 1995 near the White House. I refer to transcript 824, 13 November 2006. He managed to recognise him from a photograph where the face of General Zivanovic was not captured at all, but only the back of his head. It is P2324. Nobody else had seen General Zivanovic in Potocari either on 12th or 13 July. As such, the recognition of Popovic and Zivanovic given by Rutten is not credible and was carried out contrary to the rules explained in this proceeding by Professor Wagenaar. He explained the difference between identification and recognition, plus the importance of the perception of the witness of a person at the site. Professor Wagenaar testified that the identification of the person with his back towards camera might be misleading. I refer to transcript 8th September 2008, pages 367 to 369. Professor Wagenaar finally explained the phenomena of how the memory of a witness gets worse over time, but despite this he produces new facts about an event he could not remember earlier. The professor explained that despite the fact that the recollection of the memory goes down, the confidence of the witness goes up. It's transcript page 370 to 371. The Defence submits that this phenomenon actually occurred with Witness Rutten as regards the identification of Popovic and Zivanovic from the aforementioned photograph. It is very interesting that the Witness Rutten did not protest or complain to Popovic about alleged abuses he noticed in White House, although he allegedly noticed him during his second visit there and was aware that he was not an ordinary soldier. It is transcript 29 November 2006, pages 805 to 806. He also did not complain to the other individual from the same photograph who, according to him, was in charge of the whole process in Potocari and who allegedly, on the 13 July afternoon, was around the White House too. It is transcript 7 December 2006, page 225 to 227. In addition, the witness failed to mention this event or the persons he identified in his October 1995 witness statement. It's transcript 4 December 2006, page 1995. He did not also mention either in Krstic or during the proofing session in this case that the person he recognised gave instructions to the soldiers, despite the fact that this recollection had not improved in the last ten years. It's transcript page 220 to 221. As the intelligence officer for the DutchBat, he must have been aware that 28 Brigade, consisting of more than 1.000 soldiers, had its command in Potocari. However, he concealed this fact by saying that, I quote: "There are no real B and H soldiers around that is shelling -- well, there are no real B and H soldiers around, and there weren't any at the time, and there were no B and H positions near the Potocari area." He corroborated his testimony by stating that there were only civilians wearing normal civilian clothes, although he must have been aware that ABiH troops in the enclave also performed their tasks in civilian clothes and that 1300 -- 300, sorry, ABiH members were inside UN compound in Potocari. I refer to page 830 to 831, transcript -- it is transcript 30 November 2006. The Defence denies that Popovic was aware of the extent of the abuse of the Muslim population by Serb soldiers or that he encouraged them in acts of intimidation and physical violence, as the Prosecution states in paragraph 2408. The Prosecution did not prove that the scale of abuse and killing in Potocari was such that Popovic had to be aware of them. There were at least 20.000 people in Potocari at the time. The evidence states that nine bodies were found near Budak in the woods, far from the main road. It is P2172 -- 79, sorry. And one Muslim was taken behind White House on 13 July and executed. This would mean that ten people were killed. That number, as well as the place where their bodies were allegedly found, do not indicate that the extent of the abuse and killing in Potocari was such that Popovic had to be aware of them. There is no evidence that Popovic was in position to observe serious abuses and crimes committed by VRS members. There is no evidence that he was present to any physical maltreatment, theft of goods, or similar events. In addition, there is no evidence that he was reported about such incidents. He was, therefore, not in position, as the Prosecution state, to take uncompromising action and prevent the crimes. There is no rule prohibiting an army from detaining suspected members of the enemy's forces during a war. The crucial point is that security organ had nothing to do with the detention of suspected members of the enemy forces or the establishment of their identity, unless it was explicitly ordered or sought by his superior. Popovic, in his capacity of the security organ of the Drina Corps, had no duties or responsibilities for the detention or treatment of prisoners of war in Potocari. The security organs, in general, were authorised to interview prisoners of war if they could provide relevant information related to the enemy secret activities against VRS or actions from within the army itself. I refer to expert report of Vuga, paragraph 434, and his testimony 30 June 2008, pages 052 to 053. However, it was left on their assessment and other information if they deemed that a particular prisoner could be in possession of such kind of information. Again, Vuga, 082 to 084, same transcript. Popovic did not interview any prisoner of war because he deemed that they could not provide such information, information about enemy's intents and plans, their combat activities, or facts pertaining to other crimes was within the competence of the intelligence or commands of the units or military police. For example, Momir Nikolic brought Resid Sinanovic to the witness Zlatan Celanovic in Bratunac Brigade military police in order to investigate if he participated in war crimes against the Serb population. I refer to transcript 21st April 2009, page 932 to 933. He also did not assess that Sinanovic [realtime transcript read in error "Zivanovic"], who had a significant position in B and H authority, was in possession of information relevant for his counter-intelligence or intelligence work. There was no evidence that identification of detainees could be done through sight of their identity documents. These documents were issued by the authorities in the enclave without any centre control or confirmation of their authenticity. In addition, many of the Muslims discarded their identification documents, although they were not required to do so. According to the statement of Witness van Duijn, the area around the bus station was full of passports and other papers. I referred -- I refer to van Duijn testimony, 28th September 2006, page 352 to 354.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, I don't mean to interrupt you, but at page 56, if you see at line 6, it makes reference: "He also did not assess that Zivanovic ...," and I know that's not the name that you mentioned, who held a significant position in the B and H authority. I wonder if you could repeat that name so we have it on the record. I think it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sinanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Sinanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The name is wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Resid Sinanovic, yes. The selection and screening of the arrested people was performed through the checking of their hands, fingers smelling of gunpowder, inspection of their clothes. I refer to Rutten, 13 November 2006, page 896, line 21, to 898, line 1. The screening was carried out over a period of more than one day at different locations. Again, Rutten, same transcript, 853, line 13, to 855, line 16. Many of them -- sorry, the last reference is 7 December 2006, page 264, lines 12 to 17. Many of them had ammunition and left in front of White House. The ammunition exploded when the pile was burnt. It was testified by Franken on 17 October 2006, page 578. In addition, many prisoners were interrogated in the White House. Again, Rutten, 30 November 2006, page 857. Because of that, the submission of the Prosecution that there was no -- not screening or investigation of arrested people is unsubstantiated. The Prosecution states that Popovic knew of significantly -- knew of, significantly contributed to, and shared the intent with the other JCE members to participate in the JCE to murder Muslim men from Srebrenica. The Prosecution submits that Popovic was aware that the purpose of the arrest and capture of Bosnian Muslim men in the column was to execute them.
