For such submission, the Prosecution relies upon the -- upon two communications of General Tolimir - it's paragraph 2416 - alleging that General Tolimir directed Drina Corps security organs to propose to brigade commands that all measures to capture the enemy soldiers from Srebrenica should be taken. The Prosecution mis-characterises the communications from General Tolimir sent to the subordinated intelligence and security organs as evidence that Popovic, I quote: "... would have been provided with information concerning prisoners," as well as that he had been directly involved in organising and implementing any corresponding measures. Two communications convey information by General Tolimir about the movement of 28 Division and Muslim armed group after the fall of Srebrenica and alerted all the subordinate units about the threats against the civilian population and VRS combat units that could emerge along their routes. I refer to P148, penultimate paragraph. He directed intelligence organs to propose measures to be taken by commands to prevent armed Muslims from illegally reaching Tuzla and Kladanj, such as setting up ambushes along the routes in order to arrest them. The second communication directed the security organ of the brigades to propose to the commanders of the units deployed along the line of withdrawal of 28 Division to undertake all measures to prevent the withdrawal and to capture the enemy soldiers. It's P149, page 1, last paragraph. The communication warned that special attention should be paid to monitoring the gaps on the VRS forward defence line and possible escape routes along the corridors, as well as to the possible sudden attacks on residential areas, rear combat disposition elements, and defence elements. This means that nothing in the two communications spoke about intent to murder prisoners, but only about need to prevent the 28 Division from reaching B and H-held territory and endangering VRS and the civilian population en route. However, these communications, as well as the communications 4DP111, are significant for other reasons. The communications sent by General Tolimir to Popovic were addressed to the IKM of the Drina Corps in Bratunac, meaning that on 12th July Popovic was at the Drina Corps IKM in Bratunac. This corroborates the Bratunac Brigade document booking a room for him for 11 and 12 July. When the Stupcanica 95 order for the attack on Zepa was issued, the IKM of the Drina Corps was moved to Krivace, so the IKM in Bratunac was closed and the further stay of Popovic became unnecessary. Secondly, the document 4PD111 demonstrates that the information and instruction of General Tolimir to MUP was conveyed by General Krstic, and not Popovic. This clearly indicates that Popovic was not authorised to coordinate with MUP, but that all communication with MUP remained in the hand of General Krstic, who commanded the units taking part in the Krivaja 95 operation. Thirdly, the messages of General Tolimir clearly warned of sudden attacks on civilian and military targets that could be carried out by the forces of the 28th Division on their way towards B and H-held territory. It meant an increased danger from sabotage and terrorist enemy groups. The detecting and preventing of such activities was in the exclusive competence of Popovic, making his presence in the critical areas necessary as soon as the route of withdrawal of the enemy forces was established. The Prosecution has not proven that Popovic knew for abuses, ill treatment, the failures to provide adequate food -- adequate food and water for the prisoners in Konjevic Polje, Sandici, and Nova Kasaba. He was not duty-bound or ordered by his commander to undertake this responsibility. I refer to paragraphs 2429 to 2431 of Prosecution final brief. The Prosecution submits that Popovic was present at the meeting in Bratunac Brigade on 13 July at 9.30 and that he was informed about prisoners Momir Nikolic and Srdjan Jankovic saw in -- around Konjevic Polje. At 9.30 on 13 July, Popovic was not present at any meeting in the Bratunac Brigade headquarter. The Prosecution relies on Momir Nikolic's statement of fact and Vasic dispatch concerning the meeting held with Mladic on the morning of 13 July, during which the role of MUP in the ongoing evacuation of the civilian population to Kladanj was discussed. Momir Nikolic was not also present at the meeting and had no knowledge that Popovic was there. The communication by Vasic did not also mention that Popovic was present. However, it demonstrated that Popovic had no task in coordination of the MUP. Otherwise, Vasic would have received his task from Popovic, not Mladic, as he stated. The assertion of the Prosecution - it is paragraph 2423 to 2428 - that on 13 July 1995, I quote: "Popovic must have been involved in assigning Srdjan Jankovic to drive UN APC to Konjevic Polje, having been present at the time and as Momir Nikolic's professional superior," is pure speculation, not confirmed either by Nikolic or anyone else. Also, there is no evidence that Popovic was apprised of Jankovic and Nikolic observations and activities in and around Konjevic Polje. In paragraphs 2423 to 2434, the Prosecution states that Popovic actively implemented the command decision to kill the Bosnian Muslim men and boys of Srebrenica, since the prisoners presented a security threat. However, there is no evidence that counter-intelligence measures were required to deal with such threat. In fact, for the neutralisation of such threats, only adequate forces were needed to guard them, meaning that only physical security was necessary for which the security organs have no capacity to implement. Again, I refer to Vuga, 30 June 2008, page 082 to 084. There is no evidence that Popovic was assigned to undertake the above task. As already told, on 11 July, the president of Republika Srpska, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, assigned Miroslav Deronjic to ensure, I quote: "... that all civilian and military organs treat all citizens who participated in combat against the VRS as prisoners of war and ensure that the civilian population can freely choose where they will live or move to." Deronjic was authorised to appoint his assistant for this purpose. The decision came into force on the same day. This means that from 11 July 1995, Deronjic and his assistants were exclusively in charge of the prisoners of war and all the Muslim civilians from Srebrenica. He was only one authorised by the supreme commander to ensure that all civilian and military organs treat prisoners adequately. The term "ensure" meant that all the other organs listed in the document should act upon the commissioner's request because the president had entrusted him with the authority to implement his decision about prisoners of war. I refer to Vuga, 2nd July 2008, page 218. As already said, Popovic was not present in Bratunac on the night of 13 and 14 July and he was not registered at Hotel Fontana on these dates. There is no evidence that Popovic was with Beara on 13 July in Bratunac or communicated with him at the time about prisoners-related issues. General Krstic did not leave Popovic in Bratunac because Popovic was in Vlasenica on 13 July, working on the counter-intelligence security of General Mladic, who came to Vlasenica that afternoon to be present for the hand-over of duties between General Zivanovic and General Krstic and prepare the counter-intelligence security for the newly-established Drina Corps IKM for the Zepa operation. I refer to Vuga, 3rd July 2008, transcript page 234 to 235, and Bjelanovic, transcript 10 June, 267 to 269. As already said, Popovic was not present in Bratunac -- sorry. Popovic did not contact Drago Nikolic on the 13 July 1995 at about 1900 or 2000 hours at the IKM of the Zvornik Brigade, as described in paragraph 2435. He did not tell Nikolic anything about prisoners, their coming to Zvornik, organisation of their transfer, and that someone would be sent to provide Nikolic with further information. It is unsubstantiated that Popovic, by virtue of his position, knew about the detention, abusing, and murder of the prison ers. Whoever gave such an order was not bound to inform Popovic of it, being without troops under his command or any other necessary resources for the purpose. And given his position as the only security officer in the Drina Corps Command competent to carry out counter-intelligence work, such information would be unnecessary and pointless. Also, whoever executed such order, he had no duty to report to Popovic, but to the superior who issued the order. He had no responsibility for prisoners in Bratunac because such responsibility, since 11 July 1995, was explicitly assigned to the civilian, Commissioner Deronjic and his authorised assistants. There is no sufficient and credible evidence to show that Popovic was in Zvornik on 14 July 1995, at approximately 800 hours, and had a meeting with Beara [realtime transcript read in error "Deronjic"] and Nikolic. The Prosecution sees the meeting as a follow-up of the ostensible Popovic conversation with Nikolic which never took place. The Defence address the testimony of Bircakovic in paragraph 494 and 495 of its final brief and sticks to these arguments. The uncertainty of Bircakovic testimony is demonstrated in his report of -- the uncertainty of Bircakovic's testimony is in his response, that -- I quote: "People from the Drina Corps attended the meetings with Drago." It is transcript page 044, lines 22 to 23, 7 May 2007, meaning that at least two or more people from the Drina Corps met Nikolic and that there was more than one meeting between him and unknown persons from the Drina Corps. The witness testified that it was him who waited for the buses on 14 July 1995 at Vidikovac Motel and led them to Orahovac school. He did not indicate Popovic or a Golf leading such convoy, as stated in paragraph 489 of Defence final brief. In addition, the witness said to Dean Manning in 2002 that his recollection of Popovic was foggy, meaning that his recollection of Popovic presence was not credible enough. It's transcript 8 May 2007, pages 094 to 095.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just a moment. While we are still on the page, page 63, line 2, that "Deronjic and Nikolic" is obviously a mistake. If I remember, I heard you say "Beara and Nikolic." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Beara and Nikolic, not Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that needs to be corrected. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Finally, he did not say, in his interview to the OTP, that such meeting ever took place on the 14 July 1995. Again, same transcript, page 097, lines 12 to 17. May we move again to the private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sure. Let's go into private session for a short while, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Defence denied in its final -- oh, sorry, sorry, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, we are in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The arguments of the Defence have been reinforced, meanwhile, with the Prosecution submission that at the same time when Popovic allegedly led convoy of buses from Bratunac to Orahovac - it is paragraph 2464 of the Prosecution final brief - Popovic was in Dragasevac, in the base of the 10th Sabotage Detachment. In fact, the Prosecution asserts that Popovic was in Dragasevac on 14 July 1995, between 1000 and 1200 hours. It is paragraph 2469. The Prosecution also alleged that the person whose contemporaneous description and rank clearly matched of Popovic was seen by the PW-101 at the execution site at Orahovac. The person had side-arms, and to strengthen its argument, the Prosecution referred to the Srebrenica trial video depicting that Popovic, on 12 July, had side-arms too. The Prosecution also found that the presence of Popovic, I quote, at least "at one other execution site at Bisina," the Defence clearly indicated in its final brief that the testimony of the Witness PW-101 was untrue as regard his presence at the execution site in Orahovac and saving the life of the PW-105, hiding him in his van from the other soldiers who allegedly would kill him. It is in paragraph 224 and 496 to 512. In short, the witness had a good reason to be untruthful

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The side-arm was the obligatory element of the equipment for all officers of VRS. Many of them could be seen at various videos and photos bearing side-arms. Significantly, the Prosecution did not put a question to the witness in order to get more details concerning the identity of the alleged lieutenant-colonel. It is the submission of the Defence that it was not done because such efforts would be negative for the Prosecution case. Because of that, the Prosecution opted to leave it unclear and to stray to the conclusion that this person was Popovic. As to rank, the witness did not say that a man was lieutenant-colonel, but lieutenant-colonel or the colonel at most. He described that person as the tall man, but Popovic, he's not tall. He described that person as good-looking man, but Popovic was not good looking. His testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if Popovic is not tall, how would you classify me --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd be restrained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- or yourself?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Or myself? Also restrained.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: (redacted). Only after the members of the Zvornik Brigade left the van, PW-101 drove the wounded boy to the Zvornik hospital upon the order of Sreten Milosevic. It is transcript 15 July 2009, page 984, lines 16 to 24. According to the hospital record, it was midnight between 14 and 15 July 1995. PW-101 did not go to Orahovac to transport food and drink for the soldiers, but to take assistant commander for logistics for the Zvornik Brigade, Sretan Milosevic, to Orahovac. Namely, he testified that he called the brigade from a house in Orahovac and sought the duty officer to send a car to fetch him back to Zvornik. It's again same transcript, page 982 to 983.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. McCloskey, I suggest you have a look at from line 22 of page 66 to where we are now and see whether there is any inherent risk of revealing the PW-101's identity. Just come back to me when you can. Thank you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness lied at least on six points: First, that he was sent to Orahovac by Pantic; second, that proposal of his travel was to transport the food and drink to the Zvornik Brigade soldiers who were there - I refer to transcript 22nd February 2007, lines [sic] 564, lines 5 to 15; that he was sent by Sreten Milosevic to bring the food to the soldiers at the execution site - it's transcript page 569 to 571; that he was at the execution site at the main access road to Krivace and Kitajnica or Orac and saw the execution there, including the known and unknown persons he allegedly saw there, including the lieutenant-colonel or colonel who commanded to the execution squad, and insisted on the killing of the wounded boy - it is the same transcript, page 580 to 590; that he saved the life of the boy, but from the person and/or other soldiers of the brigade, by transporting him directly to Zvornik hospital - it is also page 584; that there were no other members of the Zvornik Brigade in his van and that it happened in the dusk. The witness testified that at the point that he arrived at the execution site, he was told by a soldier that in another meadow there were executions carried out and that the other meadow was full of corpses, and they could stop firing upon people there, and that they moved to that other meadow "where you were located at the time" - it is page 720, lines 15 to 21 - such statement is in clear contravention with the testimony of survived victims, as analysed in the Defence final brief in paragraphs 403 to 408. However, the Prosecution -- 503 to 508. Sorry. However, the Prosecution submits that on 14 July, between 8.30 and 9.30 p.m., the Witness Srecko Acimovic allegedly spoke with Popovic, who was in the Zvornik Brigade. The witness was -- allegedly said by the Zvornik Brigade duty officer that Vujadin Popovic had arrived -- sorry. May we have a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I was going to suggest it. We'll have a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The witness was allegedly said by the Zvornik Brigade duty officer, I quote: "... that Vujadin Popovic had arrived just at the very moment." It is page 939, lines 18 to 25, transcript 20th June 2007. However, just at that time, or precisely around 8.30 p.m., PW-101 got the task to go to Orahovac. In that same span of time he departed to Orahovac, stayed in front of the school, spoke with Drago Micic and Sreten Milosevic, waited the soldiers to take food and drink he had allegedly brought, and watched the embarking of the prisoners who would be transported to the execution site. It means that in that span of time he was watching the execution and saw the officer similar Popovic there. In the paragraph 2452, the Prosecution misquoted the testimony of Tanasko Tanic when he stated that he saw Popovic at the Orahovac school. The witness testified that standing at the road, he saw Popovic in the yard and these people were unknown to him. He was told by a military policeman that one of them was Popovic. He could not tell what the man looked like at the time, nor did he know his rank. It is transcript 23 April 2007, page 337 to 338. According to Bircakovic, Popovic arrived there half an hour after the prisoners arrived. This evidence is in clear contradiction with the testimony of PW-138, who said that Popovic led the convoy and reached Orahovac before the prisoners. It also endorses the Defence submission that Popovic did not lead the column of buses with prisoners because he would have arrived at Orahovac before the prisoners and not half an hour after them. May we move again into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sure. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Defence denies that there were over 1.000 prisoners in Rocevici school. None of the witnesses confirmed that, and the indictment states that there were approximately 500 prisoners in that school. The drastic increase of the number of prisoners in the school the Prosecution bases on the ICMP DNA update report from March 2009. The evidence of the Witness PW-142 is not reliable, since he just glanced inside the gym, so that he just think that the number was the same to the number of those in Orahovac. I refer to transcript page 462, 29 January 2007. However, it contains the obviously erroneous conclusion founded on the wrong generalisation that DNA connection established between primary and secondary grave-sites automatically means that all victims from these secondary graves were brought there from the same primary grave-site. I refer to Dunjic witness statement, 1D1447. So according to Janc's conclusion, on the basis of 54 DNA connections found in secondary graves, he concluded that all 708 bodies were brought there from Kozluk. In respect of paragraph 2478, there is no evidence that the meeting that Witness PW-165 testified about took place on 15 July 1995. On the day the ostensible meeting was held, PW-165 was working at the check-point in Rocevici until 17 hours, but he did not see any transport of prisoners to Kozluk. It clearly indicates that this date is wrong. The Defence expounded the testimony of this witness in paragraphs 520 to 522 of its final brief, and therefore maintains its position that PW-165's testimony on the identification of Popovic was erroneous. The Defence also analysed all evidence related to the alleged Popovic activities related to the detention, transportation, execution, and burial of victims in the Kula-Konjic-Branjevo area. It is in paragraph 229 to 294 of the Defence final brief. Sorry, 529 to 594. The Defence denies the specific allegation by the Prosecution that Popovic was engaged at Kula school in the morning of the execution. The Defence also analysed the testimony of Slavko Peric in paragraph 540 to 542 of its final brief, who did not confirm that Popovic was present at Kula school, but a person who looked like him. He also testified that he thinks that one soldier called the shorter of the two officer with nickname "Popovic." The witness said that he believed that he heard Popovic. However, this evidence is not reliable for establishment of Popovic presence in front of the Kula school because the witness was not able to confirm that Popovic was present at the school, although he knew him, or that he was addressed with his -- with the nickname "Pop." In addition, the last name Popovic is common in the area, so that one of the members of the 10th Sabotage units, Velimir Popovic - I refer to Adamovic testimony for May 2007, page 946, lines 20 to 15 - had the same last name. The member of this unit was also Boris Popov, who could have had the same nickname. I refer to Dorovic testimony, 21st August 2007, page 040, lines 8 to 12. The submission of the Prosecution that Popovic was at the Kula school is not corroborated by the evidence mentioned in the OTP final brief. The Defence analyses all this evidence. The fuel issue was addressed in paragraph 543 to 562, the entry in the paragraph 563 to 566, and intercept evidence in 567 to 594 of its final brief. Neither of them confirms Popovic present at the Kula school, as the Prosecution submits, by coordinating the execution of the Muslim prisoners at Pilica. The Defence stays behind its arguments, pointing out that they are reinforced with the testimonies of Ljubo Rakic and Branko Bogicevic, and absence of any evidence that Popovic was seen at Branjevo Military Farm. None of the Prosecution witnesses, and I refer to Slavko Babic, Jevto Bogdanovic, Pero Petrovic, Drazen Erdemovic [realtime transcript read in error "Obrenovic"], testified that they saw Popovic at the Kula school or at Branjevo. The Prosecution also brought the witnesses who participated in burial of the victims, and none of them testified they got any order or instruction from Popovic or that he even saw him at that place. I refer to the Witness Damjan Lazarevic. In respect, the paragraph 2528 and 2529, where the Prosecution stated that Popovic issued the direction to the chiefs of intelligence and security in the Drina Corps formation, banning indefinitely all reporters and cameramen from entering the Republika Srpska, the Defence submits that it is normal that filming and the recording during wartime is restricted, as well as the movement of foreign citizens, including journalists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Line 5 of this page -- in this page, 75, amongst the witnesses that supposedly you mentioned --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- is Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Not Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It was Erdemovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Erdemovic, Drazen Erdemovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Erdemovic. Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Defence indicates that a similar ban was imposed by the ABiH. I refer to 1D1091. So the commander of the ABiH 2nd Corps issued the order after noticing an increased activity by UNPROFOR and foreign journalists to collect information on ABiH forces and possible plans for their deployment. In order to prevent such activities, he issued the order forbidding such persons to pass through from temporarily-occupied territory and to travel from B and H-controlled territory to temporarily-occupied territory. They were also banned to travel to the zone of responsibility without written approval of the 2nd Corps Command. Popovic was not present at the execution in Bisina. The testimony of PW-172 was not accurate as regard Popovic presence during the execution. The vehicle log - it is P197 - reflects that Popovic on that day left Vlasenica at 900 hours in the morning to Zvornik. The purpose of his travel to Zvornik was described in details by the Witness Vlasic. He recounts that their conversation in Zvornik was suddenly interrupted, and Popovic left Zvornik only after a telephone call. Popovic emerged at Bisina two hours after the trucks where the prisoners had arrived. This was confirmed by Witness Kojic and Coric. PW-175 testified that he wrote in his vehicle log the names of officers who signed it, upon the request of the finance chief who was not able to recognise signatures. He did it with block letters after his chief who assigned him the task identified the signatures. He also confirmed all the assignments he got from his chief. This means that it was not Popovic who was in charge of operation, as the Prosecution erroneously interprets from his testimony. He did it when he submitted the vehicle log to the chief of finance who asked the witness to identify the signatures on the vehicle log. It was not questioned who was in charge of the operation, because the witness never stated that he knew of that. This submission is corroborated by two of Popovic's other signatures for his assignment in July 1995. It was done for the days when he had not assigned related to any kind of security jobs or transportation of the prisoners or the members of 10th Sabotage units, indicating that the signature was given just because Popovic was the only available officer at that moment in the Drina Corps Command. The witness clearly testified that he did it only when -- only where the Popovic signatures were, but also for all days he drove the mini-bus in July 1995. I refer to transcript page 796, 25 of March, 2009. The Prosecution's assertion that evidence related to Bisina confirms Popovic presence at Branjevo Military Farm on 16 July 1995 is quite unsubstantiated. In the final brief, paragraphs related to the Popovic individual criminal responsibility related to the Pilica-Branjevo execution, the Prosecution never mentioned that Popovic was present at the Branjevo Military Farm, but only at the Kula school and Pilica. There is no evidence that Popovic was at Branjevo Farm at all. There is not a single witness who testified to this or a single document confirming such an allegation. The Defence considers that the evidence related to Bisina on 23rd July could not be used to confirm the charges against Popovic on all execution sites where the Prosecution was not able to prove his role and presence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much more do you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will be finished by the end of the day, if you permit me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How long has he already taken, time-wise, how much time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You've exceeded the time-limit by already seven minutes. Let me confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, by way of exception rather than establishing a rule, we are allowing you to go on up to five to seven minutes before the scheduled end of the sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, leave us five to seven minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Prosecution did not even prove that any member of the Drina Corps military police was present at the Branjevo Military Farm, but that some soldiers had such insignias. In the light of the testimonies of Bjelanovic and Racic, it is clear that such insignias were worn by almost all former members of the Drina Corps military police who were redeployed to the other units, so the soldiers noticed at Branjevo Military Farm were not actual members of the Drina Corps military police because at the time Drina Corps military police was deployed at Kocari on combat operation and only a small number of them were available for military police tasks in Vlasenica. The Prosecution asserts that Popovic organised the transportation and execution of the Bisina victims, despite evidence indicating to the contrary. Popovic vehicle log indicates that he departed Vlasenica for Zvornik on 23rd July 1995 at 9.00 in the morning. It is P197. On that day, Popovic did not carry out counter-intelligence tasks. He was in civilian classing and had to meet the commercial manager of the Vezionica factory which produced the uniforms and insignias for the Military Police Battalion. They had to resolve the problem with insignias sowed on the uniforms because the soldiers, when they deployed, went with these uniforms and insignias to other units, they were seen by others as the members of the Drina Corps military police, despite the fact that they had ceased to be its members. It was as a result of this that the route of travel was written on Popovic log on this particular day, since the places for the performance of counter-intelligence tasks were not usually disclosed to members of the corps command. This was also done on 3rd July 1995, when Popovic travelled to Ljuboja. The intercept referred to by the Prosecution - it's P1313 - indicates that Popovic had already left Vlasenica at 9.04 that morning. However, the Prosecution's interpretation, that it also reflects that Popovic went to Sekovici, to the Lieutenant-Colonel Racic, is unsubstantiated and contrary to the evidence. The Popovic vehicle log demonstrates that Sekovici was not the place he intended to visit on the specific day. There is no evidence that Popovic contacted Lieutenant-Colonel Racic on that day. The witness statement of Slavisa Racic, however, confirms that he met with Popovic in Zvornik. It was before noon but he could not say precisely when, and their meeting lasted about half an hour. It's 1D48. The preparation for the transportation of prisoners to Bisina started at 8.30 with the fueling of truck PW-172 drove on the day. The truck later proceeded to Bisina, where the executions and burials of victims took place. At that time, PW-175 left Vlasenica to Bisina and got back to Vlasenica at 10.15. It is P4432. At 10.30, he travelled again on the Vlasenica-Sekovici-Bisina-Sekovici route, and the minivan transported the 10th Sabotage Detachment -- if the minivan transported the 10th Sabotage Detachment members, it means that they left Bisina before noon on 23rd July, 1995. It further means that the passengers on the minibus completed their task at Bisina before the noon and went back immediately. It was confirmed by PW-172. It's transcript 10 March 2009, page 573, lines 7 to 10. The Witness PW-172 testified that the executions took place very fast and that as soon as that was done, they went back and sat in the car, and they left the location. Although it is not clear what kind of car was at the location which the execution used to leave, it is most probable that they did so immediately after they completed their task. According to the witness Vlasic, Popovic suddenly interrupted his visit after a very short telephone conversation, he was seen in civilian clothes at the building site of the Bisina barracks in early afternoon, inquiring with the two witnesses, Kojic and Coric, as to whether they saw where the military trucks went. The place was at the junction of the road. As such, he required information to determine where they went and thereafter followed the direction indicated by the witnesses. Cojic stated that Popovic arrived at the building site in Bisina about 1300 hours. It is 1D1439. Kojic also stated that Popovic came to Bisina building site between 13 and 14 hours. It is 1D1446. If Popovic was there early in the morning, as the Prosecution asserts, he would not seek information as to where the trucks went. He would know the place of the execution. However, the whole event obviously became known to him after his telephone conversation at Vlasic's office from the Vezionica Zvornik, and he managed to arrive at the location only when the executions had been completed but the burial was underway. The Defence submits that PW-172 was not only in a state of shock, but also in a state of fear of his own criminal responsibility due to his acts and conduct. At the time of the execution, he was present with the two young soldiers upon the oral order of his commander. Apart from them, there were the unknown soldiers from 10th Sabotage unit who left the place immediately after the execution and also an unknown driver of the machine performing the burial. At the time, he felt that he would be -- he could be responsible for the events, given that none of the officers was present. The coming of Popovic was a kind of relief. He could protect himself because of Popovic's position of authority, although he was not present at the executions. The testimony of this witness obviously confirms that Popovic did not organise the transportation and execution of the 39 Muslim prisoners at Bisina. The witness agreed with the position of the Defence, that Popovic did not have anything to do with the transportation of the prisoners from Susica and Sekovici to Bisina. It is transcript page 598, lines 2 to 7. The witness, in another part of his testimony, clearly indicates that Popovic did not organise the execution of Bisina victims. The witness testified that when he asked Popovic after the execution what happened, that Popovic did not answer. The witness saw the tears in his eyes. It is the submission of the Defence that an individual who organised the execution and who worked to complete such a task would not cry once he completes his task. The tears in Popovic's eyes which the witness spoke of indicate that execution of these Muslims was a shocking surprise for Popovic too. The Defence would also like to explain why the Popovic vehicle log for 23 July 1995 does not indicate his travel to Bisina. The vehicle log was filed in advance at the beginning of the trip, when he did not expect that he would go to Bisina. This also indicates that he did not participate in organising the transport and execution of Bisina victims. In the paragraph 2538, the Prosecution submits that Popovic implemented the command decision to kill the wounded from the military hospital. It refers to two intercept conversations and the testimony of PW-168. The content of the quoted intercepts was inaccurately and incompletely presented. In the first conversation, Pandurevic sought instructions as regard both prisoners and the wounded. The part of the conversation in respect of wounded was transcribed with considerable gaps. I refer to P1309. The next conversation refers to the previous one, by saying that Popovic would come by 1700 hours and convey what needs to be done regarding the work we talked about. This conversation did not mention the issue of the wounded prisoners alone, but also many other topics. At least four additional topics will arise in the conversation. The first relates to Sekula and Modric, the second related to something that should be returned to Kosoric, it must be ready right away. The third related to reinforcements. The fourth related to the time General Krstic had sent for Legenda. In light of the aforementioned, the part of the conversation that Popovic would convey what needs to be done regarding the work we talked about is not necessarily related to the wounded, as the Prosecution misrepresents it. May we move into private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Popovic, however, did not convey anything to Pandurevic on that or any other day. The Drina Corps Command had a better way of communication with its subordinate brigade commander, including protected communications and professional courier, than sending its assistant commander as the courier. It is, however, interesting to note how the Prosecution would like to present Popovic activities on 23rd July 1995. In the morning hours and early afternoon, he ostensibly had a very delicate task to organise the transportation, murder, and burial of victims at Bisina. Immediately after that, he was transformed in the courier between an unknown command and the commander of a subordinate unit. Such distorted presentation was far from the reality and was created just for proving the unsubstantiated charges from the indictment. In respect to the paragraph 2550, it is correct that Popovic got the task from his commander to go to Serbia and retrieve Muslim soldiers who fled there from Zepa. However, it only proves that the task related to the prisoners Popovic undertook was upon the order of his commander and only with the limits determined by him. It proves that the norms from the Rules of Service for the security organ were fully implemented and that Popovic had no tasks relating to prisoners in his purview. Popovic did not participate in the reburial operation. The testimony of the Prosecution plea agreement witness -- witnesses are not credible, as explained in Defence final brief. Popovic never managed fuel resources. However, one of the tasks of the security organ was to detect activities within the VRS against the VRS. This included the theft of fuel, because it presented the most important item for the operation of the army. (redacted) --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Redact that, and proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we move to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move to private session, please, and redact what has been stated in the last few seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecution misrepresented the ostensible intercept conversation from 22nd September 1995 which shows Popovic involvement in managing and overseeing the reburial operation in Zvornik. In that conversation, Popovic asked his collocutor whether the fuel had arrived. It's P2391. He received the information that his collocutor did not know anything about it, but that Trbic was working on it, and on that specific day he could not -- as not much of work could be done. Finally, Popovic asked the other speaker to find out if the fuel was delivered and called the gas station to check. The conversation does not reflect in any way Popovic managing and overseeing of the reburial operation, but instead the detection of abuses and illegal appropriation of fuel. The Prosecution asserts that the fuel for reburial was delivered on 14 September 1995. This conversation took place eight days later, after the fuel had been delivered. This conversation reflects Popovic interest for fuel, which was to be delivered to the gas station of the Zvornik. The fuel approved on 14 September had already been delivered to the Standard Barracks, as ordered in the document. There is, therefore, no logical conclusion that this conversation related to the same subject matter as the disbursal order for the fuel delivered on 14th September. The fuel delivered on 14th September was assigned personally to Captain Trbic for a specific task by the Main Staff commander. Accordingly, this order made Trbic responsible to commander of the Main Staff directly and personally for the execution of this task. The order did not mention that he was responsible for the performing of such tasks to anyone else but to the commander who issued the task personally. As a result, neither Popovic nor anybody else was authorised to seek any information about the fuel because they did not get such a task from the commander who issued the delivery order. This means that Popovic asked about another fuel sent for the regular needs of the Zvornik Brigade. We can -- just a moment. Sorry. In respect to the paragraph 2565, the testimony of another Prosecution plea agreement witness, Momir Nikolic, as to Popovic involvement in reburials is also false. If the fuel for the purpose was delivered to Zvornik, as was shown with the document of 14 September 1995, it would be the same also for the Bratunac Brigade. Accordingly, to the -- according to the Prosecution, in the case of Zvornik, the disbursal order was by the Main Staff commander directly to Captain Trbic, without any involvement from Popovic. In the case of Bratunac, it might have been done in the same way, meaning that it was delivered to Momir Nikolic, who got the same assignment as Trbic. The Defence addressed its position about Momir Nikolic's testimony as regard the reburials and sticks to that. I'd just like to add that Momir Nikolic, in his -- wrote in his additional statement - it is C-2 - "I helped in exhumation and reburial operation to the extent I was ordered to by my commander, Colonel Blagojevic, to whom I reported regularly at regular briefing meetings." This can be seen from the minutes of the briefing meeting of Bratunac Brigade on 16 October 1995: "In my brigade, the task order was ordered was recorded as "asanacija." I refer to page 4, last paragraph, C-2. It clearly indicates that Momir Nikolic got all his order in respect to reburials from his commander, not from Popovic. Otherwise, he would report to Popovic regularly, not his commander. He misrepresented the obligations he got, like Trbic, as regard the fuel, just to conceal his direct responsibility for reburials. Your Honours, I have just one more very short topic. It refers to ethnic animosity toward Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Very short --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Very shortly. Briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecution's submission that Popovic harboured a particular deep-seated ethnic animosity toward Bosnian Muslims because he used derogatory terms like "balija" in referring Muslims is unsubstantiated. The Prosecution has never clarified what the term "balija" means. In fact, the exact term "balija" was not known to many of the witnesses the Prosecution examined. The witness Grujic, a journalist by profession working during the Bosnian war as the correspondent of Reuters Television - I refer to his testimony, 756 page, 22 July 2008 - was not able to explain the exact meaning of the term. The exact meaning of the term could not be explained by Vuga, although he agreed that was mildly derogatory and appears in vernacular. Although such term was not appropriate in the official documents, it was commonly used in the VRS, just as the other side used derogatory terms for Serbian sides. However, it does not reflect a deep-seated ethnic animosity toward Muslims. Many witnesses in this case testified that Popovic had no hate towards Muslims and had many friends among them. Popovic was the officer of the former JNA, educated in the military schools in the spirit of fraternity and unity, as the crucial concept of the former JNA. His former superior and associates gave statements in this regard. Its reference is witness statements at 1D1318, 1320 and 1317, witnesses Mico Vlaisavldjevic [phoen], Nermin Jusufovic and Boris Mazibrada. Just for a short time, if we can move to the closed session -- to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: One of the witnesses, Nermin Jusufovic, who is Muslim, stated that he met Popovic in 1991 in the former JNA multi-ethnic unit. The witness was friends with Popovic and they socialised at the time, and he never noticed Popovic express any negative attitude towards people of other ethnicity or comment about their behaviour or character. The second witness, Popovic's former command, Mico Vlaisavldjevic, stated that he met Popovic in 1978 after Popovic graduated from the Military Academy. He was his superior from 1978 to 1992. He described Popovic as an extremely pro-Yugoslav-oriented officer without any intolerance towards many members of other ethnic groups in the unit. The witness named some of Popovic's close non-Serb friends. Finally, the witness stated that Popovic helped many people when the war broke out to get passports and leave the territory of Republika Srpska. He named some of them in his statement. Boris Mazibrada also confirmed that Popovic had very good relations with people of different ethnicity. Witness Milan Vojnovic, who had contacts with Popovic, testified that he never felt any animosity from Popovic towards other ethnic groups except towards armed formation of enemy. The witness Mikajlo Mitrovic, who was Popovic superior in the 2nd Krajina Corps testified that there were members of the other ethnic groups in that unit, but Popovic never showed intolerance towards them. Finally, the Prosecution submission of Popovic near pathological hate towards Muslim is quite inconsistent with testimony of PW-172, who saw tears in his eyes after the execution of the Muslim prisoners near Bisina. In light of the aforementioned reasons, I ask the Trial Chamber to acquit Mr. Vujadin Popovic of all charges from the indictment. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, Judge Kwon has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Kwon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was hesitating whether to ask this question or not, but I didn't find the time to ask this before. Do you remember when Mr. Svetozar Kosoric came to testify on the 30th of June? During the course of cross-examination he was shown a video in which Mr. Kosoric and Zoka and Mr. Popovic took a picture. I'm not sure whether you remember that. During the course of dialogue, Mr. Popovic said that -- to the effect of, Come on here, the entire OB is present, and then he said "the war criminals." I wonder whether you are in the position to answer in what context he said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that it was recorded when all of them were a little bit tipsy, and it was a kind of joke, according to the behaviour of all of them and according to the behaviour of Popovic himself. It was my impression. I cannot give any other details, but that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you can expand why it was a joke. You can answer the question tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's adjourn. I take this opportunity to thank the members of the staff, interpreters, technicians, and everyone, for having been patient and allowed us to sit some extended minutes. Let it also be the practice that you should alert the Trial Chamber if, at a certain point in time, it becomes obvious that you're not going to conclude in two and a half hours. I don't think we should be faced with a situation where we have to check and find out that you have already exceeded by a few minutes, and then ask you to leave us five or seven minutes, and you don't even leave us that. I don't think this should be a healthy practice in this Tribunal, and you should try to avoid it by all means. Thank you, and have a nice afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
